title: Only Tanya Is Left
subtitle: The Second World War in Europe, through diaries from Łódź to Laubach, Leningrad to Stockholm, 1939–1945
intro: On 1 September 1939 at least four people in this chapter opened a notebook or turned to a fresh page. A German court official in a small Hessian town began a secret diary that day because he wanted his grandchildren to understand how a democracy turns into a dictatorship. A fifteen-year-old Jewish schoolboy in Łódź went to bed half-dressed in case the sirens came. A young mother in Stockholm, not yet the author of Pippi Longstocking, bought tea, cocoa and soap and wrote that nobody could believe it. In London a Member of Parliament sat in the Commons and watched a Prime Minister fail to set a deadline. Six years later most of the Jewish diarists in this chapter were dead, and the people who survived were writing about cellars, rations and a surrender signed at Reims.

This chapter does not try to cover the whole war. It sets a small number of real diaries next to each other so that their dates line up: the outbreak in September 1939; the fall of France in 1940; the invasion of the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941; the Leningrad hunger winter of 1941–42; the deportations of 1942–43 from Paris, Amsterdam, Łódź and Bucharest; D-Day on 6 June 1944; the Dresden raid of 13–14 February 1945; and the fall of Berlin and VE Day in April–May 1945.

The Holocaust runs through the whole chapter, and these entries treat it with care. Dawid Sierakowiak, Hélène Berr, Etty Hillesum and Anne Frank did not survive. Victor Klemperer survived partly because of his marriage, partly because the firestorm that destroyed Dresden on the night he was to be deported also destroyed his papers. Mihail Sebastian survived Antonescu's Romania and was killed by a truck three weeks after VE Day. Their entries are written as paraphrase in their own order of knowing: what they heard, what they guessed, and what they could not yet believe.

Other vantages sit alongside them: a German anti-Nazi official recording a soldier's eyewitness account of mass shootings in 1941; two Leningrad girls who both wrote on 28 December 1941; a Berlin society journalist; an anonymous Berlin woman, now generally identified as Marta Hillers, writing in a cellar while the Red Army arrived; a Norwegian prisoner; a Swedish letter censor; and, handled carefully, the dictated diary of the Nazi Propaganda Minister, whose last entry is a bare military report. The vantage scale runs from the victims themselves to those who heard the news from a neutral capital.
Several of these texts were revised by their authors, edited by relatives or reconstructed by archivists. Each eye's authenticity note says how, and the entries give the confidence of every date.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian (New Style), which every country in this chapter used by 1939, including the Soviet Union, which had changed calendars in February 1918. Some days in the published editions are inferred: diarists often wrote in the early morning about the day before, and Tanya Savicheva's notebook gives the dates of deaths, not the dates she wrote them down. Where only a month or a range is known, the entry says so.

eyes.name: Victor Klemperer
eyes.role: Romance-languages professor of Jewish birth, dismissed from the Dresden Technical University; aged 58–63 during the war
eyes.side: German Jew in a 'mixed marriage', Germany
eyes.where: Dresden, from 1940 in a 'Jews' House' with his non-Jewish wife Eva
eyes.authenticity: Original manuscript diaries kept secretly; Eva carried pages to a friend in Pirna for safekeeping. Published in full as Tagebücher (Aufbau, 1995); English in three volumes (I Will Bear Witness 1933–41, 1942–45; The Lesser Evil). Not disputed.
eyes.bio: Klemperer was a decorated First World War veteran who regarded himself as wholly German. His marriage to Eva protected him from deportation until the last months of the war. His diary is the most detailed record of everyday persecution inside Nazi Germany, and it is also the raw material for LTI, his study of the language of the Third Reich.

sources.title: I Will Bear Witness, Vol. 1 (Random House)
World War II Today: Surviving in Dresden, 14 February 1945

eyes.name: Friedrich Kellner
eyes.role: Justice inspector (court administrator) at the Laubach district court; Social Democrat; aged 54–60
eyes.where: Laubach, Hesse, a small town under local SS surveillance
eyes.vantage_label: dissenting German at home, collecting news
eyes.authenticity: Ten notebooks, 861 pages, 676 dated entries, hidden in a compartment in the dining-room cabinet. Given to his American grandson Robert Scott Kellner in 1968. Complete German edition Wallstein 2011; English edition My Opposition (Cambridge UP, 2018). Not disputed.
eyes.bio: Kellner and his wife Pauline moved to Laubach in 1933 to escape attention in Mainz, refused to join Nazi organisations and listened to the BBC. His diary collects newspaper clippings, rumours and soldiers' talk, and comments on all of it. It is one of the earliest German civilian records of mass shootings in the East.

sources.title: History News Network on the Kellner diary

eyes.name: Dawid Sierakowiak
eyes.role: Jewish schoolboy, top of his class at a Jewish gimnazjum, later a saddlery worker in the ghetto; aged 15–18
eyes.authenticity: Five notebooks survive, running from 28 June 1939 to 15 April 1943, found after the war in the flat by its pre-war owner. USHMM holds notebooks 1, 3 and 5 (acquired 1999); the Jewish Historical Institute in Warsaw holds 2 and 4. English edition: The Diary of Dawid Sierakowiak (Oxford UP, 1996). Other notebooks are lost.
eyes.bio: Sierakowiak was a brilliant, politically committed teenager who studied five languages. He kept writing through hunger, forced labour, his mother's deportation in the September 1942 Gehsperre action, and his own tuberculosis. He died on 8 August 1943, aged 19.

sources.title: USHMM collection record: Dawid Sierakowiak diary
Holocaust Historical Society: diary extracts, September 1939

eyes.name: Astrid Lindgren
eyes.role: Stockholm secretary and mother of two; from 1940 a secret postal censor for Swedish intelligence; aged 32–38
eyes.vantage_label: neutral capital, reading other people's mail
eyes.authenticity: Seventeen notebooks with pasted press clippings, 1 September 1939 to 31 December 1945, kept in a laundry basket at her flat. Published by her heirs as Krigsdagböcker (2015); English War Diaries 1939–1945 (Yale UP, 2016). Editing minimal; some clippings omitted.
eyes.bio: Before Pippi Longstocking, Lindgren was a young mother following the war on the radio and in the papers. From summer 1940 she read foreign and military letters for the intelligence service's censorship department, which gave her an early private view of what was happening to Europe's Jews. She secretly copied some letters into her diary.

eyes.name: Harold Nicolson
eyes.role: National Labour MP for Leicester West; 1940–41 Parliamentary Secretary at the Ministry of Information; later a BBC governor; aged 52–58
eyes.where: House of Commons, London; Sissinghurst, Kent
eyes.authenticity: Typescript diary, edited with letters by his son Nigel Nicolson as Diaries and Letters, vol. 2: The War Years 1939–1945 (Collins, 1967). The edited volume is a selection. Not disputed.
eyes.bio: Nicolson was a former diplomat who had attended the 1919 peace conference and was married to Vita Sackville-West. He was close to the anti-appeasers but sat outside the inner circle. His diary records the mood of the House and of literary London, and he wrote with sympathy about France in 1940.

sources.title: Hansard Society: Parliament and the declaration of war, September 1939

eyes.name: Nella Last
eyes.role: Housewife and Women's Voluntary Service worker, mother of two sons; signed her first entry 'Housewife, 49'
eyes.where: 9 Ilkley Road, Barrow-in-Furness, a shipbuilding town
eyes.authenticity: Written for the Mass Observation project from 1939 to 1966, about 12 million words in all, roughly 2 million of them from the war. Edited selection Nella Last's War (1981; reissued 2006). Pages for January 1944 to early May 1945 were lost before the archive moved to Sussex University.
eyes.bio: Last was a reserved, often anxious woman whom the war made into a confident organiser. Her diary covers the texture of rationing, mending and canteen work, and her worry about her sons in uniform. Victoria Wood dramatised it for ITV in 2006.

eyes.name: Mihail Sebastian
eyes.role: Romanian Jewish novelist, playwright and lawyer; aged 31–37
eyes.side: Romanian Jews under the Antonescu regime (Axis ally)
eyes.authenticity: Manuscript smuggled out of Romania by his brother in 1961, later held in Jerusalem; first published in Bucharest in 1996. English: Journal 1935–1944 (Ivan R. Dee, 2000). Not disputed.
eyes.bio: Sebastian watched friends from Romania's intellectual elite turn to fascism, and his journal records their antisemitism alongside concerts and books. During the war he recorded each new decree, levy and labour summons against Romanian Jews. He survived the war and was killed by a truck in Bucharest on 29 May 1945.

sources.title: GHDI: Excerpts from Mihail Sebastian's Journal (1938–1944)

eyes.name: Lena Mukhina
eyes.where: Leningrad, living with her adoptive mother 'Mama' and the old family friend Aka
eyes.authenticity: Diary 21 May 1941 to 25 May 1942, given anonymously to a state archive in 1962 and found there by the historian Sergei Yarov. Published in Russian as Sokhrani moyu pechalnuyu istoriyu; English: The Diary of Lena Mukhina (Macmillan, 2015/16). Not disputed.
eyes.bio: Mukhina starts as an ordinary teenager worried about exams and a boy at school. Her diary then records an educated girl being worn down by hunger, including thoughts about ration cards that she was ashamed of. She was evacuated in June 1942, survived, and lived until 1991.

eyes.name: Tanya Savicheva
eyes.authenticity: Nine entries on the alphabet-tab pages of a small notebook that had belonged to her sister Nina, written probably in blue pencil after her larger diary was burned for fuel. The original is in the State Museum of the History of St Petersburg, and a copy is at Piskaryovskoye Cemetery. Accounts conflict on whether it was shown at Nuremberg.
eyes.bio: Tanya used one alphabet page per relative to record the hour each of them died. She was found alone, evacuated in August 1942, and died in July 1944 in an orphanage in the Gorky region. Her sister Nina and brother Mikhail survived, which she never knew.

sources.title: Saint Petersburg Encyclopaedia: Diary of Tanya Savicheva

eyes.name: Hélène Berr
eyes.role: Sorbonne English-literature student and violinist from a prominent French Jewish family; aged 21–22
eyes.where: Paris, 7th arrondissement and the Sorbonne library
eyes.authenticity: 262 loose pages, 7 April 1942 to 15 February 1944, kept for her fiancé Jean Morawiecki, who gave them to her niece Mariette Job in 1994. Held at the Mémorial de la Shoah since 2002; published 2008 (English: The Journal of Hélène Berr, trans. David Bellos). Not disputed.
eyes.bio: Berr begins with Paul Valéry, Keats and string quartets and ends recording the logistics of deportation trains. She chose to wear the yellow star and stayed in Paris to help Jewish children. She was arrested on 8 March 1944, deported on her 23rd birthday, and beaten to death at Bergen-Belsen on 10 April 1945, five days before liberation.

sources.title: GHDI: A View from Paris, excerpts from the diary of Hélène Berr
NYRB: Occupied Paris, the Sweet and the Cruel

eyes.name: Etty Hillesum
eyes.role: Amsterdam law graduate, Russian tutor, from July 1942 a Jewish Council worker at Westerbork; aged 27–29
eyes.vantage_label: victim and helper in the transit camp
eyes.authenticity: Eleven exercise books from 9 March 1941 (one is lost), left with Maria Tuinzing for the writer Klaas Smelik. Abridged edition Het verstoorde leven 1981; complete Dutch edition 1986; English complete edition 2002. The Westerbork letters were published clandestinely in 1943. Not disputed.
eyes.bio: Hillesum's diary is mainly a spiritual and psychological record that began under the guidance of the psychochirologist Julius Spier, and the persecution enters it gradually. She refused offers to go into hiding and chose to share the fate of the deportees. She left Westerbork on 7 September 1943 and died at Auschwitz on 30 November 1943.

sources.title: Liberation Route Europe: Etty Hillesum and Westerbork

eyes.name: Anne Frank
eyes.role: German-born Jewish girl in hiding, aged 14 at D-Day
eyes.vantage_label: in hiding, listening to the BBC
eyes.authenticity: Original diary (version A) and her own revision for postwar publication (version B), both surviving; edited by Otto Frank as Het Achterhuis (1947). The Critical Edition (1986) settled forgery claims by forensic examination. The last entry is 1 August 1944; she was arrested on 4 August.
eyes.bio: Frank rewrote her diary in 1944 after hearing a Dutch minister in exile on the radio ask people to keep records. Her D-Day entries are full of hope and also report accurately what the BBC said. She passed through Westerbork, as Hillesum had a year earlier, and died at Bergen-Belsen in February or March 1945.

sources.title: International Churchill Society: Churchill and Anne Frank
Tim Boyce: D-Day, June 6, 1944 in three diaries

eyes.name: Odd Nansen
eyes.role: Norwegian architect, son of Fridtjof Nansen, political prisoner
eyes.side: Occupied Norway, prisoner of the Reich
eyes.where: Grini camp in Norway, then from 1943 Sachsenhausen in Germany
eyes.authenticity: Kept secretly in captivity and published in Norwegian after the war; English From Day to Day (1949), reissued with annotations by Timothy Boyce. Not disputed.
eyes.bio: Nansen was arrested in 1942 and held until the end of the war, in Grini and later Sachsenhausen. His diary records what prisoners heard by rumour about the progress of the war, including the long-awaited second front. It also records what he saw done to other prisoners, especially Jews.

sources.title: Tim Boyce: D-Day, June 6, 1944 (Nansen, Klemperer, Frank)

eyes.name: Ursula von Kardorff
eyes.role: Arts and features journalist on the Deutsche Allgemeine Zeitung; aged 31–34
eyes.side: German conservative-aristocratic milieu close to the resistance
eyes.where: Berlin, until she fled in March 1945
eyes.vantage_label: inside the capital, among the doubters
eyes.authenticity: Published as Berliner Aufzeichnungen 1942–1945 (Biederstein, 1962; English Diary of a Nightmare, 1966). The author is known to have reworked the text before publication. A later annotated edition compared it with the surviving originals, but that comparison could not be checked for this chapter, so these entries should be read as her postwar version of her wartime notes.
eyes.bio: Kardorff's friends included Fritz-Dietlof von der Schulenburg and other 20 July conspirators. The Gestapo interrogated her after the plot, and she persuaded them she knew nothing. Her diary records salons, wounded officers and bomb nights, and the defeatist talk that spread in elite Berlin.

sources.title: GHDI: Ursula von Kardorff, diary entries October–November 1942

eyes.name: Marta Hillers ('Anonyma')
eyes.role: Berlin journalist and editor, aged 33–34; spoke some Russian
eyes.where: A bombed apartment block and its cellar shelter, Berlin-Tempelhof area
eyes.vantage_label: civilian woman as the city falls
eyes.authenticity: Published anonymously as A Woman in Berlin (English 1954; German 1959). It covers 20 April to 22 June 1945. Jens Bisky named Hillers as the author in 2003; the rights holder never formally confirmed this, but no other candidate has been proposed. Walter Kempowski examined the notebooks and typescript in 2004 and judged them a genuine wartime diary, noting that material was added in the typescript. A 2016 critical study found that much of the published text is not contemporaneous.
eyes.bio: The diarist sets down in plain words the mass rapes that followed the Soviet capture of Berlin, and how women sought one officer as protection against the others. Its German reception in 1959 was hostile, and she refused republication during her lifetime. The book is central to how this subject was later discussed.

sources.title: GHDI: Female Survival in Berlin in April 1945

eyes.name: Joseph Goebbels
eyes.role: Reich Minister of Propaganda and Gauleiter of Berlin; a principal perpetrator
eyes.vantage_label: perpetrator at the centre of power
eyes.authenticity: Handwritten from 1923; from July 1941 dictated to a stenographer and typed, with an eye to publication. Microfilmed on glass plates in late 1944, and the plates were found in a Moscow archive by Elke Fröhlich in 1992. Institut für Zeitgeschichte edition, 29 volumes, 1993–2008. Historians treat it as self-serving, especially on Hitler's words. Included here only as a counter-vantage.
eyes.bio: The diary is the record of the man who ran the regime's propaganda and pushed for the deportation of Berlin's Jews. It is valuable because it is unguarded about intentions, and because it shows the gap between what he knew and what he told Germans. Its last entry, dated 10 April 1945, has no commentary at all.

sources.title: Diaries of Joseph Goebbels Online (USC Libraries)

entries.headline: A court official starts a secret diary as Poland is invaded
entries.digest: On the morning the Wehrmacht crossed into Poland, Kellner opened the first of what would become ten notebooks. He addressed it to people who would come later, so that they could see how Germans had handed themselves to a dictatorship and what that cost. He wrote in old Sütterlin script, in a flat inside the courthouse where he worked.
entries.source_note: My Opposition (Wikipedia); Friedrich Kellner (Wikipedia); Brewminate / HNN articles by Robert Scott Kellner

entries.headline: Air raids on Polish towns; a schoolboy sleeps half-dressed
entries.digest: Dawid noted that German planes were bombing several Polish towns and that Łódź was under air-raid alerts. Like many in the city, he went to bed partly dressed so that he could run for the shelter. He was fifteen, and he still sounds more excited than afraid.
entries.source_note: Holocaust Historical Society extracts from The Diary of Dawid Sierakowiak (OUP 1996), entry 1 Sept 1939

entries.headline: War breaks out; nobody can believe it
entries.digest: Lindgren opened her first war notebook by saying the thing had actually happened. Only the day before, she and a friend had joked in Vasa Park that there would be no war. She had held off on stockpiling until now and that day bought cocoa, tea, soap and a few other things. She described a heavy gloom over the whole city, the radio always on, men called up and private motoring banned.
entries.source_note: War Diaries 1939–1945 (Yale UP 2016), entry 1 Sept 1939; Wikipedia; Diaries of Note; astridlindgren.com

entries.headline: Chamberlain's message to Berlin has no deadline
entries.digest: In the emergency sitting, Nicolson thought both sides of the House broadly approved the Prime Minister's speech. But he noticed something missing: the warning sent to Berlin set no time limit. The question of how long Britain would wait for Hitler to answer would boil over the next evening.
entries.source_note: Diaries and Letters 1939–45, as cited in Hansard Society blog 'Parliament and the declaration of war in September 1939' (day inferred from the sitting described)

entries.headline: A shout from the benches: speak for Britain
entries.digest: When Chamberlain still gave no ultimatum, the Labour deputy leader Arthur Greenwood rose to reply. Nicolson recorded Bob Boothby calling out that Greenwood, not the government, now spoke for Britain, and Greenwood nearly staggering in surprise. Afterwards an MP told him Chamberlain had left the Chamber white-faced. Britain's ultimatum expired the next morning, 3 September.
entries.source_note: Diaries and Letters 1939–45, as cited in Hansard Society blog (day inferred from the sitting)

entries.headline: Officials flee the city; the family decides to stay
entries.digest: Panic spread as Polish officials and police left Łódź. Neighbours urged the Sierakowiaks to leave with them, but the family decided to stay at home. That night a Polish army column passed through the city, going the wrong way.
entries.source_note: Holocaust Historical Society extracts, entry 6 Sept 1939

entries.headline: Days after the Germans arrive, Jews are robbed and beaten
entries.digest: Within days of the German entry on 9 September, Dawid was recording Jews seized off the street for forced digging, robbed and beaten. Some were stood against walls and fired at in mock executions. An elderly neighbour had already warned him not to go into town, so he was missing school.
entries.source_note: Holocaust Historical Society extracts, entries 10 and 12 Sept 1939

entries.headline: How did Germany choose this? A reckoning after Versailles
entries.digest: Kellner traced the line from Germany's defeat in 1918, through the Republic's failures, to the voters and elites who had raised Hitler up. He did not accept that ordinary Germans had been helpless dupes. In his view they had chosen, and they were now paying for it with a second war.
entries.source_note: My Opposition (Wikipedia), entry 17 Sept 1939

entries.headline: Every door out of Germany seems shut
entries.digest: As German troops poured into Denmark and Norway, Klemperer went over the hopeless arithmetic of emigration once more: visas, affidavits, money, his age. He and Eva were on the point of being forced from their house at Dölzschen into a 'Jews' House'. This is a quiet, bureaucratic entry about being unable to leave.
entries.source_note: Victor Klemperer (Wikipedia) cites an entry of 10 April 1940 on the difficulty of emigrating; detail paraphrased cautiously

entries.headline: André Maurois arrives; grief for falling France
entries.digest: With the German army two days from Paris, Nicolson met the French writer André Maurois, who had just reached London. He wrote that he felt France's agony very deeply. A Francophile at the Ministry of Information, he could do little more than watch the ally Britain had gone to war beside collapse in a month.
entries.source_note: Harold Nicolson (Wikipedia) quoting diary entry 12 June 1940 (original English)

entries.headline: A house search; the notebook hidden under his wife's clothes
entries.digest: In 1940, after Kellner was questioned about his 'uncooperative attitude', officials searched the family's flat. Pauline Kellner kept the current notebook hidden under her clothing, and they did not find it. Had they found it, Kellner would almost certainly have been executed.
entries.source_note: HNN article by Robert Scott Kellner (event dated only to 1940; date_iso is a placeholder mid-year for sorting)

entries.headline: A night of terror and a tin of fruit salad
entries.digest: After a night of the Barrow Blitz, Nella surveyed her house: windows blown in, ceilings down, doors splintered. Between the terror and the clear-up, what she kept coming back to was that she had never opened a treasured tin of fruit salad. She remembered a fortune-teller's old warning, recorded neighbours leaving town and a hurt dog that had to be put down. Then she opened the tin and got tea ready for her husband.
entries.source_note: Nella Last's War, entry 4 May 1941, via Diaries of Note

entries.headline: A classmate dies of hunger, the third from his year
entries.digest: A boy from Dawid's school year had died the day before of hunger and exhaustion, the third in the class. Dawid wrote it down plainly, as a fact about the class register. The ghetto had been sealed for a year, and starvation was now an ordinary cause of death among the boys he studied with.
entries.source_note: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, entry 13 May 1941

entries.headline: The radio announces war; her handwriting changes
entries.digest: Until this point Lena's diary is about school exams, friends and the boy she liked. On 22 June the radio announced the German invasion, and her normal routine broke off. The typist who later transcribed the manuscript noticed that Lena's handwriting changed sharply on this day.
entries.source_note: Literary Review 'Ration Book'; HNN report quoting transcriber Marina Rymynskaya

entries.headline: Eight days in a cell for a blackout lapse
entries.digest: As the invasion of the USSR began, Klemperer was serving eight days in Cell 89 at the Dresden police headquarters for failing to black out a window properly. He later wrote out the experience at length: the bare cell, the waiting, and how time stretched so that eight days felt like many weeks. It was a minor punishment that taught him how easily he could disappear.
entries.source_note: I Will Bear Witness 1933–41, entries for the cell imprisonment, as described in 'Foreboding Parallelisms of Today?' (cryn.substack.com)

entries.headline: Barbarossa three days old: Britain and America must act
entries.digest: With German armies racing east, Kellner wrote that the Western democracies had to stop hesitating and hit Germany hard. He saw Hitler's attack on the USSR as a gamble the regime could not win if Britain and the United States committed fully. He did not expect the regime to fall from within.
entries.source_note: My Opposition (Wikipedia), entry 25 June 1941

entries.headline: Reports that captured Red Army men are to be killed
entries.digest: Kellner recorded reports that Soviet prisoners of war were to be killed rather than held. He knew the laws of war from his years in the justice system, and he wrote it down as a crime. Millions of Soviet POWs would die in German hands.
entries.source_note: My Opposition (Wikipedia), entry 29 July 1941

entries.headline: Jewish men summoned; shops empty, prices soar
entries.digest: Six weeks after Romania joined the invasion of the USSR, police ordered Jewish men of working age to report. Sebastian described the panic, sold-out shops and soaring prices as Bucharest's Jews prepared for possible internment. He watched himself and his friends calculate what to pack.
entries.source_note: GHDI excerpts from Sebastian, Journal 1935–1944, entry 4 Aug 1941

entries.headline: First daylight raids: fires, ruins, and a vow of revenge
entries.digest: Lena described the first German daytime air raids on Leningrad: incendiaries setting flats and warehouses alight, high-explosive bombs bringing down buildings and killing people. She did not yet know that the city's last land link had been cut that day, or that the burning Badayev food warehouses meant hunger was coming. Her anger ends in a promise that the Germans will pay in full.
entries.source_note: Diaries of Note, entry 8 Sept 1941 (English phrase as widely quoted from Macmillan edition)

entries.headline: The yellow star order is withdrawn, for now
entries.digest: After the Jewish community leader Wilhelm Filderman saw Marshal Antonescu, the order requiring Romanian Jews to wear the yellow star was rescinded. Sebastian thought about what the badge meant as a mark of identity. At the Great Synagogue, where requisitions were collected, he met acquaintances he had not seen for years.
entries.source_note: GHDI excerpts, entry 9 Sept 1941

entries.headline: A Gieseking concert while Bukovina's Jews are deported
entries.digest: Sebastian went to hear the pianist Walter Gieseking and could not reconcile the music with what he knew about the same week: the Jews of Bukovina being deported east, and the labour camps. He blamed himself for having sat in the hall at all.
entries.source_note: GHDI excerpts, entry 19 Oct 1941

entries.headline: School suspended; he starts in a saddlery workshop
entries.digest: Dawid recorded that his student career was suspended, he hoped only for a while. He was going to work in a saddlery workshop, because a wage and a workshop soup mattered more than Latin. Thousands of Jews deported from Vienna, Prague and Berlin were arriving in the overcrowded ghetto that month.
entries.source_note: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, entry 23 Oct 1941

entries.headline: A soldier on leave describes Jews shot beside a pit
entries.digest: Kellner wrote down what a soldier home on leave had told him: in occupied Poland, on SS orders, Jewish men and women were made to undress and stand at the edge of a long, deep trench, and auxiliaries shot them. In the same entry Kellner wrote that most Germans shared the guilt, directly or indirectly. His family and the editors regard this as the diary's most important page.
entries.source_note: My Opposition (Wikipedia); Friedrich Kellner (Wikipedia), entry 28 Oct 1941

entries.headline: The lowest bread ration, the eve of her seventeenth birthday
entries.digest: The fifth and harshest ration cut came into force. Dependants and children now received a sliver of adulterated bread a day. Lena turned seventeen the next day. From here on her diary records food almost obsessively: each gram, each queue, each rumour of a delivery across the ice.
entries.source_note: Literary Review 'Ration Book' (gives ration cut and birthday; exact wording of her entry not verified)

entries.headline: Hoping old Aka dies after the first, for her card
entries.digest: Lena wrote that Aka, the elderly family friend sharing their room, had become just another mouth to feed. If Aka was going to die, she hoped it would be after the first of the month, so that the household could still draw her January ration card. Lena recorded the thought and, implicitly, her shame at it. Aka died on New Year's Day.
entries.source_note: Literary Review 'Ration Book', entries 28 Dec 1941 and 1 Jan 1942

entries.headline: Page Ж: her sister Zhenya dies
entries.digest: On the page for the letter Ж, Tanya wrote that her older sister Zhenya had died on 28 December 1941. The Russian gives the hour as half past midnight (some English versions say noon). Zhenya had been giving blood and working long factory shifts. This is the first of the notebook's entries.
entries.source_note: Tanya Savicheva (Wikipedia), transcription of page Ж; date is date of death

entries.headline: Page Б: Grandmother at three in the afternoon
entries.digest: Tanya recorded that her grandmother, Yevdokiya Grigorievna, had died at three o'clock on 25 January. The official death date is 1 February. The family delayed registering the death so that her ration card could be used for the rest of the month, the same calculation Lena Mukhina had confessed to a month earlier.
entries.source_note: Tanya Savicheva (Wikipedia); Saint Petersburg Encyclopaedia

entries.headline: Mama died yesterday morning. She is alone.
entries.digest: Lena's adoptive mother died on the morning of 7 February, and the next day Lena wrote it down in a few words: her mother was dead and she was entirely alone. She was seventeen, in an unheated flat, and still had to get the body out and register the death.
entries.source_note: Literary Review 'Ration Book', entry 8 Feb 1942

entries.headline: Page Л: brother Leka at five in the morning
entries.digest: Her brother Leonid, Leka, died at five in the morning on 17 March. He had worked at the Admiralty shipyard. Tanya recorded the hour as precisely as for the others. Uncle Vasya would follow on 13 April and Uncle Lesha on 10 May; for Lesha she left out the word 'died'.
entries.source_note: Tanya Savicheva (Wikipedia), pages Л and В

entries.headline: All that matters is the soup at the workshop
entries.digest: Dawid confessed that his world had shrunk to a single question: would there be soup at the workshop today? The ideas and politics that filled his 1939 notebooks have nearly gone. In the background, deportations from the ghetto to Chełmno had been running since January, though the ghetto did not know the destination.
entries.source_note: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, entry 3 Apr 1942

entries.headline: Mama at 7:30 a.m.; then 'Only Tanya is left'
entries.digest: Her mother, Mariya Ignatievna, died at half past seven in the morning. On the pages for С, У and О, Tanya then wrote three short lines: the Savichevs are dead; everyone is dead; only Tanya is left. She did not know that her sister Nina and brother Misha were alive elsewhere.
entries.source_note: Tanya Savicheva (Wikipedia), pages М, С, У, О; final three pages undated (after 13 May)

entries.headline: We are not considered human, only cattle
entries.digest: Dawid wrote that to the Germans the Jews were not people at all, only livestock to be worked or slaughtered. Nobody in the ghetto knew what had become of those deported. He was writing during the spring deportations that took the Western European Jews who had arrived the previous autumn.
entries.source_note: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, entry 20 May 1942

entries.headline: The last entry: desperate to get out
entries.digest: Lena's diary ends in late May 1942, with her trying to get onto an evacuation list. Her beloved aunt did not survive the siege. She was evacuated in June, so her diary stops at about the point when Tanya's family had all died.
entries.source_note: Lena Mukhina (Wikipedia): last entry 25 May 1942; evacuation June 1942

entries.headline: First day wearing the yellow star
entries.digest: Four days earlier Hélène had decided it would be cowardly not to wear the star. On 8 June, the first day it was compulsory in the occupied zone, she went out into Paris wearing it and recorded how people on the street reacted to her, and how she felt about it. That same day the diarist Philippe Jullian, also in Paris, wrote in his own diary about the star.
entries.source_note: NYRB 'Occupied Paris: The Sweet and the Cruel' (2009), entries 4 and 8 June 1942 (paired there with Jullian's entry)

entries.headline: Warning of a great roundup tomorrow
entries.digest: Late at night Hélène recorded a warning that about twenty thousand people were to be arrested. She described a terror spreading through Jewish Paris as the SS took over police matters in France. Her father had already been interned at Drancy for weeks. The Vél d'Hiv roundup began the next morning.
entries.source_note: GHDI document 5200, Journal of Hélène Berr (trans. Bellos), entry 15 July 1942

entries.headline: Inside the Vélodrome d'Hiver, through a friend's eyes
entries.digest: From her friend Isabelle's account, Hélène wrote out what was happening in the cycle stadium: thousands of families penned without water or toilets, the sick left untreated. She added what she had heard of packed trains leaving Drancy. Earlier that month the family had refused an offer to free her father on condition that they emigrate.
entries.source_note: GHDI document 5200, entry 21 July 1942; NYRB on 2 July refusal

entries.headline: She joins the Jewish Council and goes to Westerbork
entries.digest: As mass deportations from the Netherlands began, Etty took a post with the Jewish Council and was soon at Westerbork in the department for 'people in transit'. She could have protected herself. Instead she chose to be where the transports left from, helping the sick, women and children to pack. In the same summer, a mile across Amsterdam, Anne Frank's family went into hiding.
entries.source_note: Liberation Route Europe; Wikipedia; NYRB 'In Hell' (month only)

entries.headline: A deportation train halts at Chitila; rations cut by religion
entries.digest: Sebastian wrote about a deportation train that had stopped at Chitila, just outside Bucharest, before going on east to Transnistria, and he thought about the dead. In the same entry he noted the new food rules: Jews' bread and sugar cut, Christians' sugar left high. He put the two facts side by side without comment.
entries.source_note: GHDI excerpts, entry 10 Sept 1942

entries.headline: Defeatist talk at a party, and an SS man arrives
entries.digest: At a party in her room, given mainly for six badly wounded officers, the guests argued instead of dancing. They openly denounced the regime's church policy and its lies. An SS man and journalist arrived uninvited and heard all of it, defended the government feebly, and nearly walked out when a guest accused the authorities of suppressing the truth. Kardorff noted afterwards how dangerous such evenings were for everyone in the room.
entries.source_note: GHDI, Kardorff diary 31 Oct–1 Nov 1942 (Diary of a Nightmare, 1966, pp. 10–11; published text, postwar-revised)

entries.headline: The court constable assigned to spy on them
entries.digest: Kellner described Heinrich Scherdt, the courthouse constable told to report on the Kellners to the local SS. Scherdt ignored them except on official business and made no secret of his hatred. Kellner wrote about him with contempt. Meanwhile, at Stalingrad, the Sixth Army was eight days from surrender.
entries.source_note: Brewminate and HNN articles by Robert Scott Kellner, entry 23 Jan 1943

entries.headline: Final entry: there is really no way out
entries.digest: The last surviving notebook ends with Dawid sinking into melancholy and writing that there was really no way out for them. He had just won a sought-after bakery job, but he was already feverish. His mother had been taken in the September 1942 action, and his father had died. Dawid died on 8 August 1943, aged nineteen.
entries.source_note: USHMM finding aid and Encyclopedia: final entry 15 April 1943

entries.headline: A postcard thrown from the train
entries.digest: Etty was put on a transport east with her parents and brother. From the moving train she threw out a postcard, which farmers found by the track and posted. She quoted a psalm from a Bible she had opened at random, thanked her friends, and told them they had left the camp singing. Her parents were killed on arrival at Auschwitz; she died there on 30 November.
entries.quote: We have left the camp singing
entries.source_note: Etty Hillesum (Wikipedia); NYRB 'In Hell'; Liberation Route Europe (one source gives 27 Sept for her own deportation, but the standard account and the postcard date it 7 Sept)

entries.headline: People do not know; telling is a duty
entries.digest: Hélène wrote that the people around her simply did not know or imagine what others were suffering. If ignorance was what allowed it to go on, then writing it down was a duty. From this autumn her journal changes from a private notebook into testimony meant for her absent fiancé and for later readers.
entries.source_note: NYRB 2009 review, entry 10 Oct 1943

entries.headline: Last entry: the arithmetic of a deportation wagon
entries.digest: From an acquaintance's account of a week at Drancy, Hélène set down the logistics: about sixty people to a wagon, straw on the floor, one slop pail or three, rations for a six-day journey. It is her last entry. She and her parents were arrested at 7 a.m. on 8 March and deported on 27 March, her 23rd birthday.
entries.source_note: GHDI document 5200, entry 15 Feb 1944; Wikipedia; NYRB

entries.headline: Wedding anniversary in bed; press reports of German atrocities
entries.digest: Ill in bed on her thirteenth wedding anniversary, Lindgren wrote about what she was reading and about the papers. She reflected on the Swedish press coverage of German atrocities. Two weeks earlier she had followed the Finnish–Soviet peace talks while her daughter Karin had measles.
entries.source_note: Yale UP excerpt of War Diaries, entries 20 March and 4 April 1944

entries.headline: 'This is D-Day': the Annex hears the BBC
entries.digest: The people in hiding first assumed the landings were a feint, but by mid-morning the BBC had convinced them. Anne copied out what she heard: the noon announcement, the one o'clock English bulletin with its figures for planes and landing craft, Churchill's statement. She asked whether this was really the start of liberation. She wrote that hope gave them new courage and that she might be back at school by autumn.
entries.source_note: International Churchill Society article; Tim Boyce; teachinghistorymatters.com (quote is the BBC's words as she recorded them)

entries.headline: Eva is thrilled; he stays cold, unable to hope
entries.digest: Eva brought the news of the invasion home and was excited. Klemperer recorded that he himself stayed cold. After so many false dawns he no longer dared hope, or could not yet. He still wore the star and was one of the few Jews left in Dresden.
entries.source_note: Tim Boyce, 'D-Day: June 6, 1944' (quoting Klemperer's entry)

entries.headline: One word, written large: Finally!
entries.digest: Kellner had been urging an Allied invasion in his diary since 1941, and he wanted the war fought on German soil if that was what it took. When the BBC confirmed the landings in Normandy, he wrote a single word in large letters across the page.
entries.source_note: Friedrich Kellner (Wikipedia), entry 6 June 1944

entries.headline: The second front: thunder from a clear sky
entries.digest: News of the landings reached Nansen's camp by rumour and smuggled radio, and he wrote that it came like thunder from a clear sky. The second front the prisoners had waited for since 1942 had begun. He would remain a prisoner for almost eleven more months.
entries.quote: came like thunder from a clear sky
entries.source_note: Tim Boyce, 'D-Day: June 6, 1944' (From Day to Day, English 1949); camp per Nansen's biography (moved from Grini to Sachsenhausen in 1943)

entries.headline: Churchill in liberated France, and she envies his nerve
entries.digest: Anne recorded the BBC report that Churchill had toured newly liberated French villages with Smuts and Eisenhower, and had been on a warship shelling the coast. She thought he did not know what fear was and envied him. Days earlier she had written admiringly that he had wanted to land with the troops. She thought he was about seventy; he was sixty-nine.
entries.source_note: International Churchill Society, 'Churchill and Anne Frank', entries c. 9 June and 13 June 1944

entries.headline: Germany collapsing; what he wants is freedom
entries.digest: Three weeks after Romania changed sides and the Red Army entered Bucharest, Sebastian took stock. He had survived, and the relief was real. But he wrote that what he longed for was not simply safety. It was freedom itself, which he did not yet trust the new order to give.
entries.source_note: GHDI excerpts, entry 16 Sept 1944

entries.headline: Made to deliver deportation notices to the last Jews
entries.digest: Klemperer was among the few Jews still left in Dresden, almost all in mixed marriages. That day he was made to carry the official letters ordering most of them to report for 'labour deployment' in three days. Everyone understood what that meant. His own name was on the list. That night the RAF arrived.
entries.source_note: World War II Today, 'Surviving in Dresden'; Klemperer (Wikipedia); I Will Bear Witness 1942–45

entries.place: Dresden, the Elbe meadows and burning old town
entries.headline: Firestorm night; Eva cuts the star from his coat
entries.digest: The night raid separated him from Eva in the chaos, and they found each other again only in the morning. In the confusion she removed the yellow star from his overcoat, so that he could pass as one more homeless German. Tens of thousands of identity papers had burned. The diary survived, and so did he. The Americans bombed again shortly after midday. Days later the couple fled the city under a false identity.
entries.source_note: World War II Today, 'Surviving in Dresden'; Wikipedia gives 19 Feb for his final escape from the area

entries.headline: Why Germans did not overthrow the regime
entries.digest: With the Americans across the Rhine at Remagen, Kellner wrote out why Germans had not risen against the Nazis: terror, conformism, and too many people who were profiting or complicit. His conclusion was that only outside force could end the regime. Three weeks later American troops entered Laubach.
entries.source_note: My Opposition (Wikipedia), entry 7 March 1945; Laubach occupied 29 March 1945

entries.headline: The Propaganda Minister's last entry is only a situation report
entries.digest: The last surviving entry in the Goebbels diary contains only a military situation report and no comment from him. For eighteen years the diary had recorded his ambitions, his hatreds and his part in planning the persecution of Europe's Jews. Its last voice is a dictated list of lost positions. Three weeks later, on 1 May, he and his wife killed their six children and themselves.
entries.source_note: Goebbels Diaries (Wikipedia): last entry 10 April 1945, a situation report only

entries.place: Berlin, borrowed attic flat and cellar
entries.headline: Hitler's birthday; first line of a cellar diary
entries.digest: Bombed out of her own flat, she was living in a borrowed attic and sleeping in the cellar during raids. Food was running out, money was nearly worthless and her publishing house had collapsed. Rumours of starvation and of what Soviet soldiers did to women were already circulating. It was the Führer's 56th birthday, and the guns could be heard to the east.
entries.source_note: A Woman in Berlin (Boehm trans., Picador), entry 20 April 1945, per SuperSummary Part 1 synopsis and Wikipedia

entries.headline: 'Day of catastrophe': the soldiers come into the cellar
entries.digest: She headed the entry, written the next morning, as a day of catastrophe and wild turmoil. Drunken Red Army soldiers came through the building. She was raped, and that night four men broke into the widow's apartment where she was staying and she was assaulted again. She wrote it down in short, flat sentences. Within days she was looking for a single officer whose presence would keep the others off.
entries.source_note: GHDI document 5171 (excerpt headed 'Friday, April 27, 1945'); SuperSummary Part 1; published text partly revised after the war

entries.headline: Rumours that Hitler is dead; the assaults go on
entries.digest: Rumours of Hitler's death spread through the cellar on the day he in fact killed himself. For her it changed nothing. She was assaulted again; men from the lieutenant 'Anatol''s unit intervened; another officer pestered her until dawn. The headline news of the war and the conditions in her cellar no longer had anything to do with each other.
entries.source_note: SuperSummary synopsis of A Woman in Berlin Part 1, entry 30 April 1945

entries.headline: Surrender signed at Reims; Stockholm celebrates
entries.digest: Lindgren recorded that the German surrender had been signed at Reims. Stockholm erupted in crowds. In her office, colleagues sang the Norwegian national anthem after a radio broadcast, and she drank a celebratory sherry with friends. She added that she would not want to be a German now.
entries.source_note: astridlindgren.com, 'Astrid Lindgren och andra världskriget', entry 7 May 1945

entries.headline: Surrender day: no amnesty for the harmless bystanders
entries.digest: On the day of Germany's unconditional surrender, Kellner wrote that the Nazis' supporters, who were now claiming to have been harmless onlookers, should face the consequences. Anyone who tried to revive National Socialism, he wrote, should be treated as a madman. He was already helping the Americans remove Nazis from local office, and his diary ended nine days later.
entries.source_note: Friedrich Kellner (Wikipedia), entry 8 May 1945; My Opposition: last entry 17 May 1945

entries.headline: The last entry, as her fiancé comes home
entries.digest: The published diary ends on 22 June, four years to the day after the invasion of the Soviet Union. Her fiancé Gerd had come back from the war, and she stopped writing around the time of his return. The diary was first published, anonymously and in English translation, in 1954.
entries.source_note: A Woman in Berlin and Marta Hillers (Wikipedia): entries end 22 June 1945; Gerd's return

convergences.label: Germany invades Poland
convergences.note: The first day of the war looks different from each place. Kellner starts writing for posterity. Sierakowiak, the only one of the four in the target country, is mostly excited and listens for sirens. Lindgren buys groceries in a neutral capital and wonders at the general gloom. Nicolson watches Parliament and notices the missing deadline. Only the Łódź boy was in physical danger that day, and only he was dead four years later.

convergences.label: Operation Barbarossa: Germany and its allies invade the USSR
convergences.note: Within the same week, a Leningrad schoolgirl's handwriting changes, a Jewish professor sits in a Dresden police cell for a blackout offence, and a Hessian official urges London and Washington to strike. Six weeks later Romania, which joined the invasion, calls up Bucharest's Jewish men. The same invasion is a distant event for one of them and an immediate threat for the others.

convergences.label: Leningrad hunger winter, the deadliest weeks
convergences.note: On the same Sunday, two Leningrad girls who never met wrote about death. Seventeen-year-old Lena admitted she hoped old Aka would die after the first of the month, to keep her ration card. Eleven-year-old Tanya wrote down the hour her sister died. A month later Tanya's family delayed registering her grandmother's death for the same reason Lena had given.

convergences.label: Summer of deportations: Vél d'Hiv, Westerbork, Łódź
convergences.note: Between May and September 1942, deportations were running in Paris, the Netherlands, Łódź and Romania at once. Berr gets the roundup warning the night before Vél d'Hiv; Hillesum takes a post at Westerbork; Sierakowiak writes that Jews are seen as cattle; Sebastian records a train stopping at Chitila. None of them could see the whole system they were caught in.

convergences.label: D-Day: Allied landings in Normandy
convergences.note: Four people heard the same BBC news under four different kinds of captivity. Anne, in hiding, copies out the figures and imagines going back to school. Klemperer, wearing the star in Dresden, refuses to hope. Kellner, a free man watched by the SS, writes one word in triumph. Nansen in his camp calls it thunder from a clear sky. Of the four, only Anne did not live to see the war's end.

convergences.label: The Dresden raids
convergences.note: A single-eye convergence, included because of its double meaning: the same evening the city's last Jews were told to report for deportation, the bombing that killed tens of thousands also burned the records that would have identified Klemperer, and he escaped.

convergences.label: The fall of Berlin and the end of the Reich
convergences.note: In the regime's capital, the Propaganda Minister's diary ends on 10 April with a bare situation report, while a woman in a cellar a few miles away records the arrival of the Red Army and repeated rape. In Laubach, Kellner has been under American occupation since late March and thinks about accountability. In Stockholm, Lindgren drinks sherry for the surrender. The same end of the war is liberation, defeat or relief, depending on where it is seen from.

ties.note: Both were Jewish women in Amsterdam in the same years, and both were held at Westerbork transit camp, Etty in 1942–43 and Anne in August–September 1944. Both kept diaries that their friends saved.
Both died at Bergen-Belsen in the spring of 1945, Anne in February or March and Hélène on 10 April, five days before the British arrived.
They were two Leningrad girls in the same hunger winter. Both wrote on 28 December 1941, and both recorded the ration-card calculations that the famine forced on families.

Klemperer collected Nazi language in his diary and later published LTI, a study of the regime's vocabulary in which Goebbels's propaganda is a central subject. Goebbels was the regime's chief author of that language.

Both were German First World War veterans who kept secret diaries against the regime, one as a Jew in Dresden and one as a Social Democrat official in Hesse. They never met. Both wrote in the same flat, factual way about the dates of persecution.
Both were Berlin journalists of the same generation. Kardorff fled the city in March 1945, and Hillers stayed and wrote the city's fall from a cellar.
Goebbels was Gauleiter of the Berlin in which Hillers was hiding. His diary goes silent on 10 April and hers starts on 20 April, so their two records barely overlap.

Neither knew the other, but each read other people's words to find out the truth: Lindgren read censored German letters in Stockholm, and Kellner listened to soldiers' talk and the BBC in Laubach. Both learned earlier than most what was being done to Jews in the East.

Both were Jewish writers under Axis rule, but in very different conditions. Sebastian's Bucharest still had concerts and synagogues, while Sierakowiak was in a sealed ghetto. Sebastian survived the war, and Sierakowiak did not.

Both recorded the D-Day news as a turning point, Nansen in a prison camp and Anne in hiding. Their accounts are set side by side in Timothy Boyce's comparison of three D-Day diaries, together with Klemperer's.

threads_out.note: Klemperer and Kellner were both First World War veterans, and Kellner's diary begins by blaming the way Germany handled its 1918 defeat for Hitler. Harold Nicolson had been a junior diplomat at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference whose settlement this war overturned.

Leningrad was Petrograd, the city of the 1917 revolutions. Lena Mukhina and Tanya Savicheva were children of the Soviet state that came out of it, and the Soviet Union's switch to the Gregorian calendar in 1918 is why their dates need no conversion.

Germany invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941, almost exactly 129 years after Napoleon's Grande Armée crossed the Niemen on 24 June 1812, and Soviet propaganda deliberately called the new war a second 'Patriotic War'.
VE Day on 8 May 1945 left the Pacific war still running. The area bombing used against Dresden in February was also used against Tokyo in March, and the war ended with the atomic bombs in August.

The war in Asia had been running for two years before 1 September 1939. Nanjing's diarists, including the German John Rabe, recorded the same kind of mass violence against civilians that Kellner heard about in 1941.

Anne Frank's diary exists in two versions, her original and her own revision for publication, and it was later forensically examined to answer forgery claims. Its history connects to the book-wide theme of how diaries are revised, hidden, lost and authenticated.

vantage_key: 0 = direct victim or principal actor (ghetto, siege, hiding, deportation, cellar, or the Nazi leadership itself); 1 = persecuted eyewitness in a capital not yet under total terror; 2 = home front under the bombs or in the enemy capital; 3 = same country or captivity, learning by news and rumour; 4 = neutral country, hearing it all from afar.
